Complementary information — The documents provide different, non-contradictory details about California smog check triggers: registration renewal, biennial cycle, vehicle age thresholds, and sale transfers.

The evidence clusters by different triggering events and conditions. d1, d3, d7, and d8 state smog checks are required upon registration renewal or vehicle sale [d1, d3, d7, d8]. d3, d6, and d7 specify a biennial (every two years) cycle for most vehicles [d3, d6, d7]. d2, d3, d6, and d7 list various age-based exemptions (e.g., pre-1976, under 4 or 8 years old) [d2, d3, d6, d7]. These details are complementary, each adding a piece to the overall answer without contradiction.

The combined evidence from multiple documents yields a complete answer. d1 and d3 establish the primary triggers: initial registration, renewal, and sale [d1, d3]. d3 and d7 specify the biennial cycle for ongoing registration [d3, d7]. d2, d3, d6, and d7 add critical context on exemptions based on vehicle age, model year, and fuel type [d2, d3, d6, d7]. Together, they provide a multifaceted answer to the query.

In California, a car generally must be smog checked during its initial registration and upon every biennial (every two years) registration renewal [d3, d7]. A smog check is also required when a vehicle is sold, unless it is less than four model years old [d1, d3, d7]. Exemptions apply to gasoline-powered vehicles model year 1975 or older and, for newer vehicles, specific age-based exemptions exist (e.g., under four or eight years old depending on context) [d2, d3, d6, d7]. These requirements apply in many California counties, particularly those with air quality issues [d6].
